title: The Window · 3
paragraphs: “Perhaps you’ll wake up and find the sun shining and the birds singing,” she said tenderly, smoothing the little boy’s hair. She could tell that her husband, with his biting remark that it wouldn’t be fine, had crushed his spirits. Going to the Lighthouse was a passion of his, she saw. And then, as though her husband had not said enough with his biting remark that it wouldn’t be fine tomorrow, this hateful little man had to go and rub it in all over again.
“Perhaps it will be fine tomorrow,” she said, smoothing his hair.

The only thing she could do now was praise the refrigerator and leaf through the Stores catalogue, hoping to come upon something like a rake or a mowing machine, whose prongs and handles would take the utmost skill and care to cut out. All these young men were parodies of her husband, she reflected: he said it would rain; they said it would be a full-blown tornado.

But here, as she turned the page, her search for the picture of a rake or a mowing machine was suddenly interrupted. There had been a gruff murmur, broken now and then as pipes were taken out and put back in, which had kept assuring her, though she could not hear what was said (sitting as she was in the window), that the men were talking happily. This sound had gone on for half an hour now, and had taken its soothing place in the scale of sounds pressing in on her, such as the tap of balls on bats, and the sharp, sudden bark now and then, “How’s that? How’s that?” of the children playing cricket. And it had stopped. That left only the monotonous fall of the waves on the beach. For the most part the waves beat a measured and soothing rhythm to her thoughts, and seemed to repeat comfortingly over and over, as she sat with the children, the words of some old lullaby, murmured by nature: “I am guarding you—I am your support.” But at other times, suddenly and unexpectedly, especially when her mind lifted itself a little from the task actually in hand, they had no such kind meaning. Instead, like a ghostly roll of drums, they beat out relentlessly the measure of life, made you think of the island being destroyed and swallowed by the sea, and warned her, whose day had slipped past in one quick task after another, that it was all as fleeting as a rainbow. Now this sound of the waves, which had been muffled and hidden under the other sounds, suddenly thundered hollow in her ears and made her look up with a rush of terror.

They had stopped talking; that was the explanation. In a single second she fell from the tension that had gripped her to the opposite extreme, which, as if to repay her for the feeling she had wasted, was cool, amused, and even faintly malicious. Poor Charles Tansley, she concluded, had been dropped. That mattered little to her. If her husband needed sacrifices (and indeed he did), she cheerfully offered him Charles Tansley, who had snubbed her little boy.

For one moment more she listened, her head raised, as if she were waiting for some habitual sound, some regular mechanical sound. And then she heard something rhythmical, half spoken, half chanted, starting up in the garden as her husband paced up and down the terrace, something between a croak and a song. She was soothed once more, reassured that all was well, and looking down at the book on her knee she found the picture of a pocketknife with six blades, which could only be cut out if James was very careful.
Suddenly a loud cry, like a sleepwalker’s, half awake, something about
Stormed at with shot and shell

shouted out with the fiercest intensity right in her ear, made her look round anxiously to see whether anyone had heard him. Only Lily Briscoe, she was relieved to find; and that didn’t matter. But the sight of the girl at the edge of the lawn, painting, jogged her memory: she was meant to be holding her head as still as she could for Lily’s picture. Lily’s picture! Mrs. Ramsay smiled. With her little Chinese eyes and her puckered-up face she would never marry; nobody could take her painting very seriously; but she was an independent little creature, and Mrs. Ramsay liked her for that. So, remembering her promise, she bowed her head.
